fleetingNotes.topic: The Path in the Therapist’s Office
fleetingNotes.rawCapture: "A calendar image in my therapist’s office caught my attention. It shows a wooden path running through sand and tall grass toward a quiet beach, framed by palm trees and sunlight. I need to write a story or poem based on how the image came to me in that moment—not simply describe the scene, but explore why I noticed it, what I felt while looking at it, and what the path seemed to be opening toward.
notes: Begin with the image hanging in the therapist’s office rather than beginning on the beach.
Explore why this particular image held my attention at that moment.
The wooden path may suggest movement, transition, escape, return, healing, or uncertainty, but do not decide its meaning before writing.
Consider the contrast between sitting in the office and looking out at an open landscape.
The sunlight enters strongly from the left while the path continues toward a calmer horizon.
Ask whether the path feels like an invitation, a memory, a destination, or something I am not yet ready to enter.
The story or poem should come from my emotional response to the image, not from a generic description of a tropical beach.
Possible opening thought: I noticed the path before I noticed the sea.

sources.title: Tilly Norwood’s New Movie Rekindles Hollywood Concerns That AI “Actor” Is Just Ripping Off Human Performances
sources.author: Corbin Bolies
sources.copiedText:
Tilly Norwood’s New Movie Rekindles Hollywood Concerns That AI ‘Actor’ Is Just Ripping Off Human Performances

Particle6 TV

The news of Tilly Norwood’s feature-length movie debut again brought out the digital pitchforks surrounding her existence, with commenters weighing in on everything from the concept of an AI actress leading a film to why entertainment outlets such as Variety covered the news. 

Norwood’s creator is taking the backlash in stride, insisting that she’s just trying to show the industry the art of what’s possible with the tech.

AI-focused studio Particle 6 announced Monday that it was in production on “Misaligned,” a comedy-drama Norwood will “star” in that will combine human crewmembers with AI tools.

Eline van der Velden, founder and CEO of the London-based company, told Variety via email that the intention behind the feature is to “demonstrate where AI is at — and upskill and bring as many people as possible from the industry with us into the future.”

“More people than ever before are hearing and understanding that message,” she said, claiming there’s been a “noticeable uplift” in interest from creatives since the announcement. “And if we can get more people working in AI and future-proofing their roles, a little criticism won’t matter.”

Whether people in the entertainment industry really are receptive to that message is open for debate. Many of the associations representing professionals in the biz showed little desire to discuss Norwood’s film debut. But what’s clear is that some in Hollywood see the Norwood persona as a persistent threat and continue to question whether the AI “actor” has been trained on content without permission or compensation.

In a statement to Variety, U.K. performers’ union Equity said that when “it comes to the use of AI avatars — whether that’s ‘Tilly Norwood’ or any others — there are concerns about how a digital replica or avatar was created” and that it believed “transparency, consent and remuneration are key to addressing AI use in the film, TV and audio industries.”

“While data scraping and untraceable training data sources continue, the questions of theft and misuse will persist,” Cathy Sweet, Equity’s head of film and TV, said in a statement. “Actors, voice artists and performers of all kinds are left vulnerable to their work being stolen and used without their consent or even knowledge. This isn’t OK and it has to stop.”

Because Norwood is not a person, she “can’t really be a performer,” said Ted Tremper, interim executive director of the Creators Coalition on AI whose co-founders include the Daniels, Natasha Lyonne and former Academy president Janet Yang.

“It’s a character that’s created from that’s an assemblage of a tremendous amount of unseen extracted creativity and the name, image, and likenesses of people who haven’t been credited or compensated for the work that it took to create,” Tremper said, adding that she posed the question of “whether or not people know how it’s made and whether or not the human beings whose work was extracted to create it are being respected and paid.”

Representatives for the Writers Guild of America and the Directors Guild of America, two unions representing Hollywood’s legion of scribes and filmmakers, did not respond to Variety’s requests for comment on the news about a Norwood-led film. The Motion Pictures Editors Guild declined to comment for now about the prospect of editors working on a film featuring Norwood, while the Hollywood performers’ union, SAG-AFTRA, pointed to its past statements on Norwood’s emergence, one of which called her the “synthetic construct generated by software trained on the work of countless professional performers, real human beings, whose work was taken without permission, without credit and without compensation.”

According to van der Velden, Norwood was not “based on any specific person’s likeness” and instead created through “original prompting, thousands of iterations and substantial human creative oversight” along with “openly available tools — which draw on everything ever uploaded to the internet — including my own work as an actress.” Norwood will only appear in films created by AI, she said, not those featuring real people.

“Yes, we agree, Tilly isn’t a person,” van der Velden added. “She is an AI actor, a character created by Particle 6 to highlight, demonstrate and teach people about AI.”

Nearly a year after Norwood broke into public view with van der Velden’s claim that talent agencies were eager to represent the AI performer, one talent agency partner told Variety they couldn’t “imagine the complexities of representing a synthetic actor like a Tilly, given that that’s not a person.” Agencies including WME and Gersh also have bucked at the thought. Van der Velden said Particle 6’s conversations with talent agencies ceased after September and the company doesn’t believe one is necessary at the moment.

Tremper said he could imagine a future where AI usage isn’t vilified and synthetic or duplicated actors emerge with proper compensation. However, he said, doing so would require “a tremendous amount of good faith” collaboration between those making and using the technology.

“Once we actually, as a society, understand the ways that things are made, we are able to form a consensus,” he said, such as through voting or community organizing. “I think the most insidious thing that happens is that the people who make these [AI] tools, services and characters want to convince the audience that they don’t have a choice or that they don’t have self-determination, and that all of this is inevitable, and that is extraordinary. That is demonstrably false.”

The tug-of-war surrounding Norwood’s existence comes as the industry continues to grapple with generative AI. Reactions in the business have ranged from ostracization to tepid curiosity — and all the way to wholesale embrace, all while studios try to enforce regulations that protect humans’ likenesses and jobs.

Illumination CEO Chris Meledandri, speaking to Variety at the “Minions & Monsters” premiere just before word of Norwood’s feature-film debut came out, said his team was “complete believers in the human imagination” and felt “no pressure to push AI into our pipeline.”

“I wish I had a crystal ball,” Meledandri added. “I wish I could understand where it’s going, and I worry about the future of work across all industries.”

Marc Malkin contributed to this report.
sources.summary: The article discusses renewed concerns surrounding Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated actor created by Eline Van der Velden’s company, Particle6. Norwood is set to appear in the feature film Misaligned. The project is presented by its creator as an attempt to demonstrate what can be created with AI technology, while critics argue that AI-generated performances may imitate or draw from the work of human actors. The article places the project within the wider debate over artificial intelligence, creative work, performers’ rights, and the future use of AI-generated actors in filmmaking.

sources.title: New to Haiku: For Beginners
sources.author: Sarah Welch
sources.summary: An introductory guide to haiku covering sensory observation, seasonal reference, and the two-part structure of the poem. sources.title: New to Haiku: Kire and Punctuation
sources.summary: An article explaining kire, or the cut, as a central structural and aesthetic technique in haiku. The cut creates space between images and helps establish the relationship, contrast, or movement between the poem’s parts. It also discusses how punctuation can help represent the cut in English-language haiku.

sources.title: The History and Artistry of Haiku
sources.author: Patricia Burleson
sources.publisher: Stanford Program on International and Cross-Cultural Education
sources.summary: An educational overview of the history and practice of haiku. It discusses major Japanese haiku poets, including Bashō, and provides guidance for writing haiku through concrete observation, sensory imagery, brevity, and seasonal reference. It also cautions against forcing English haiku into a strict seventeen-syllable structure because English sound units differ from Japanese sound structure.

sources.title: New to Haiku: Haiku Basics
sources.summary: A central collection of educational resources about haiku. The page organizes material on haiku terminology, kire and punctuation, kigo, moments in haiku, negative space, editing, and one-line haiku. It can serve as a broader reference map for continuing the study of haiku structure and practice.

outputs.title: The Voice of the Park
outputs.purpose: A poem centered on the park as a speaking witness to memory, movement, solitude, and shared human presence.
outputs.body:
The Voices of the Park
Darrell Barrow
© 6/30/2026

Green spaces,
as they're called.
Parks. 

Each carries a unique color;
timbre.
										
Its emotions vary
throughout the day.

The park is
the canvas.

Mornings,
cool and open.

A few exercise
in the fresh air.

Passersby stop with breakfast
before gathering for work—
sometimes.

Traffic flows in syncopation
with the stoplight.

Light high in the sky.
Humidity moderated
by the trees.

Voices rise.
Accents mix.
Children laugh.
Chess tables fill.

Some—
smoke weed.
Others converse and rest.

Wind carries:
Weed,
Food,
Barbecue.
Occasional stench.
Sewer.
Garbage.

Occasionally,
soccer practice takes the field.
Public events assemble.
"Shakespeare
in the park."
Music plays in the background
like Goldilocks,
not too loud,
not too soft,
just right.

Light lowers.
Backpacks pass through.
Others arrive with bicycles,
basketballs,
scooters.

Chess tables fill
with teenagers
talking about the day.

A group leaves,
another takes the seats.
A chorus of voices,
the choir of youth.

Light fades.
The air lighter.
Reprieve
echoes through the trees.

Paper pause,
book closed—
Time to go home.
outputs.description: How the park has many voices throughout the day.

snapshot.title: Bajan Green Seasoning Tare
snapshot.mainIdea: A ramen seasoning base built from Bajan green seasoning and a Japanese tare structure, using soy, mirin, rice vinegar, sugar, and chicken stock to control the broth's salt, acidity, umami, and herbaceous identity.
snapshot.body:
Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Bajan Green Seasoning Tare

Cuisine: Caribbean-Japanese Fusion — Barbadian Focus

Course: Condiment

Category: Ramen Base Seasoning

Dietary Considerations: Contains soy

Yield: 1 cup, 8 fluid ounces, or 240 milliliters

Serving Size: 2 tablespoons, 1 fluid ounce, or 30 milliliters

Prep Time: 10 minutes

Cook Time: 5 minutes

Chill Time: 0 minutes

Rest Time: 15 minutes

Total Time: 30 minutes

Flavor Profile

Taste: Deep umami, herbaceous, lightly salty, citrus-balanced

Aroma: Thyme, scallion, soy, garlic

Mouthfeel: Lightly viscous, smooth, coating

General Description

A refined ramen seasoning base built from Bajan green seasoning, enhanced with Japanese umami components to anchor broth flavor and define the dish’s identity.

Suggested Price

$0.80–$1.50 per portion

Menu Description

Bajan herb tare with soy, aromatics, and umami depth.

Origins

Combines Barbadian green seasoning with the Japanese tare system used to season ramen broth.

History

Tare is the backbone of ramen flavor in Japanese cuisine. This adaptation replaces traditional tare aromatics with Bajan green seasoning to create a unique identity.

Cultural Significance

This is where fusion becomes intentional—blending structure through Japanese tare with identity through Bajan seasoning.

Techniques

Reduction

Flavor concentration

Balancing salt, acid, and umami

Controlled infusion

Equipment

Small saucepan

Whisk

Fine strainer

Measuring spoons

HACCP

H1: Proper refrigeration after preparation

H2: Cross-contamination prevention

H3: Temperature control during cooking

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Sauce briefly heated to at least 74°C

CCP2: Refrigerated promptly and stored at or below 5°C

Ingredients

½ cup / 120 milliliters Bajan green seasoning, prepared

¼ cup / 60 milliliters soy sauce

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters mirin

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters rice vinegar

1 teaspoon / 5 grams sugar

½ cup / 120 milliliters chicken stock

Instructions
Combine the green seasoning, soy sauce, mirin, rice vinegar, sugar, and chicken stock in a small saucepan.
Bring to a gentle simmer, whisking to combine.
Reduce slightly for 3–5 minutes to concentrate the flavor. Do not over-reduce.
Taste and adjust the balance between salt, acid, and herbs.
Strain lightly for a smoother texture, if desired.
Cool and refrigerate immediately.
Rest for 15 minutes before use to allow the flavors to integrate.
Plating and Use

Use 1–2 tablespoons at the base of the ramen bowl.

Do not pour the tare over the finished bowl.

Notes

This controls the entire dish—too much makes it salty, while too little leaves it flat.

Green seasoning provides the identity.

Tare provides the structure and control.

That is how the seasoning system functions within the ramen bowl.

Storage

Refrigerate for up to 5 days.

The tare can be prepared in batches.

Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Bajan Green Seasoning Tare

Cuisine: Caribbean-Japanese Fusion — Barbadian Focus

Course: Condiment

Category: Ramen Base Seasoning

Dietary Considerations: Contains soy

Yield: 1 cup, 8 fluid ounces, or 240 milliliters

Serving Size: 2 tablespoons, 1 fluid ounce, or 30 milliliters

Prep Time: 10 minutes

Cook Time: 5 minutes

Chill Time: 0 minutes

Rest Time: 15 minutes

Total Time: 30 minutes

Flavor Profile

Taste: Deep umami, herbaceous, lightly salty, citrus-balanced

Aroma: Thyme, scallion, soy, garlic

Mouthfeel: Lightly viscous, smooth, coating

General Description

A refined ramen seasoning base built from Bajan green seasoning, enhanced with Japanese umami components to anchor broth flavor and define the dish’s identity.

Suggested Price

$0.80–$1.50 per portion

Menu Description

Bajan herb tare with soy, aromatics, and umami depth.

Origins

Combines Barbadian green seasoning with the Japanese tare system used to season ramen broth.

History

Tare is the backbone of ramen flavor in Japanese cuisine. This adaptation replaces traditional tare aromatics with Bajan green seasoning to create a unique identity.

Cultural Significance

This is where fusion becomes intentional—blending structure through Japanese tare with identity through Bajan seasoning.

Techniques

Reduction

Flavor concentration

Balancing salt, acid, and umami

Controlled infusion

Equipment

Small saucepan

Whisk

Fine strainer

Measuring spoons

HACCP

H1: Proper refrigeration after preparation

H2: Cross-contamination prevention

H3: Temperature control during cooking

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Sauce briefly heated to at least 74°C

CCP2: Refrigerated promptly and stored at or below 5°C

Ingredients

½ cup / 120 milliliters Bajan green seasoning, prepared

¼ cup / 60 milliliters soy sauce

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters mirin

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters rice vinegar

1 teaspoon / 5 grams sugar

½ cup / 120 milliliters chicken stock

Instructions
Combine the green seasoning, soy sauce, mirin, rice vinegar, sugar, and chicken stock in a small saucepan.
Bring to a gentle simmer, whisking to combine.
Reduce slightly for 3–5 minutes to concentrate the flavor. Do not over-reduce.
Taste and adjust the balance between salt, acid, and herbs.
Strain lightly for a smoother texture, if desired.
Cool and refrigerate immediately.
Rest for 15 minutes before use to allow the flavors to integrate.
Plating and Use

Use 1–2 tablespoons at the base of the ramen bowl.

Do not pour the tare over the finished bowl.

Notes

This controls the entire dish—too much makes it salty, while too little leaves it flat.

Green seasoning provides the identity.

Tare provides the structure and control.

That is how the seasoning system functions within the ramen bowl.

Storage

Refrigerate for up to 5 days.

The tare can be prepared in batches.

Recipe Name: House Bajan Green Seasoning (Japanese-Adapted)
Cuisine: Barbadian (Bajan)
Course: Condiment
Category: Foundational Sauce
Dietary Considerations: Gluten-Free, Vegan
Yield: 2 cups (16 fl oz | 475 ml)
Serving Size: 2 tbsp (1 fl oz | 30 ml)
Prep Time: 20 minutes
Cook Time: 0 minutes
Chill Time: 0 minutes
Rest Time 30 minutes
Total Time: 50 minutes
Flavor Profile:
Taste: Herbaceous, savory, lightly spicy, citrus-bright
Aroma: Fresh thyme, scallion, garlic, subtle pepper heat
Mouthfeel: Lightly coarse, slightly oily, fresh

🧠 General Description:
A vibrant Barbadian green seasoning designed as a foundational flavor base for marinades, broths, and finishing oils, adapted for precision cooking and fusion applications.

💵 Suggested Price:
$0.75–$1.25 per portion

📋 Menu Description:
Fresh Bajan herb seasoning with thyme, scallion, garlic, and citrus.

🌍 Origins
Traditional Barbadian kitchens use green seasoning as a daily base for meats and stews.

📜 History
Green seasoning evolved across the Caribbean as a fresh herb marinade system, with Barbados emphasizing thyme, scallion, and balanced aromatics rather than heavy heat.

Cultural Significance
This is the backbone of Bajan cooking—flavor starts here. Every household version is slightly different, making it deeply personal and identity-driven.

🔪 Techniques
• Fine chopping or blending
• Balance of acid and aromatics
• Controlled hydration for versatility
• Flavor resting

🛠️ Equipment
• Blender or food processor
• Knife
• Cutting board
• Measuring spoons
• Storage container

🧯 HACCP Table

HACCP Code #DescriptionH1Proper herb washing and sanitationH2Cross-contamination preventionH3Refrigerated storage below 5°C

CCP Table

CCP Code #MetricIngredientPreparationCCP1≤5°CFinished seasoningRefrigerate immediatelyCCP2CleanHerbsWashed thoroughlyCCP3pH <4.6CitrusAcid balance for safety

🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime1 cup40 gScallionsRough chopped—½ cup20 gFresh thymeLeaves picked—¼ cup10 gParsleyRough chopped—4 cloves4 clovesGarlicPeeled—1 tbsp15 mlFresh gingerChopped—11Scotch bonnetSeeded (optional heat)—2 tbsp30 mlLime juiceFresh—2 tbsp30 mlNeutral oil——1 tsp5 gSalt——2 tbsp30 mlWaterAdjust texture—

📖 Instructions

  1. Wash all herbs thoroughly (CCP2) and dry well.

  2. Rough chop scallions, thyme, parsley, garlic, ginger, and pepper.

  3. Add all ingredients to blender.

  4. Pulse to a coarse paste—do not over-blend (texture matters).

  5. Taste and adjust salt and lime for balance.

  6. Transfer to container and refrigerate immediately (CCP1).

  7. Let rest at least 30 minutes before use to allow flavors to develop.

🍽️ Plating:
Serve as marinade, broth base, or finishing drizzle—do not over-plate, this is a supporting component.

📝 Notes
Keep it fresh and green—over-blending or overheating kills flavor. This should taste alive, not cooked.

🧊 Storage:
Refrigerate up to 5 days. Freeze in portions for extended use.

Menu Description

Fresh Bajan herb seasoning with thyme, scallion, garlic, and citrus.

Origins

Traditional Barbadian kitchens use green seasoning as a daily base for meats and stews.

History

Green seasoning evolved across the Caribbean as a fresh herb marinade system, with Barbados emphasizing thyme, scallion, and balanced aromatics rather than heavy heat.

Cultural Significance

This is the backbone of Bajan cooking—flavor starts here. Every household version is slightly different, making it deeply personal and identity-driven.

Techniques

Fine chopping or blending

Balance of acid and aromatics

Controlled hydration for versatility

Flavor resting

Equipment

Knife

HACCP

H2: Cross-contamination prevention

1 cup / 40 grams scallions, roughly chopped

½ cup / 20 grams fresh thyme, leaves picked

¼ cup / 10 grams parsley, roughly chopped

4 cloves garlic, peeled

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters fresh ginger, chopped

1 Scotch bonnet, seeded for optional heat

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters fresh lime juice

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters neutral oil

1 teaspoon / 5 grams salt

Instructions

  1. Wash all herbs thoroughly and dry well.

  3. Add all ingredients to a blender or food processor.

  4. Pulse to a coarse paste. Do not over-blend; texture matters.

  5. Taste and adjust the salt and lime for balance.

  6. Transfer to a storage container and refrigerate immediately.

Do not over-plate; this is a supporting component.

Keep it fresh and green—over-blending or overheating kills flavor. This should taste alive, not cooked.

revisions.content:
Recipe Name: Bajan Seasoned Chicken Ramen
Cuisine: Caribbean-Japanese Fusion (Barbadian Focus)
Course: Main
Category: Signature Dish
Dietary Considerations: Contains gluten, soy, egg
Yield: 4 servings (4 servings | 4 servings)
Serving Size: 1 bowl (16 oz | 475 ml)
Prep Time: 35 minutes
Cook Time: 1 hour
Chill Time: 0 minutes
Rest Time 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 45 minutes
Flavor Profile:
Taste: Herbaceous, savory, mildly spiced, umami-balanced
Aroma: Thyme, garlic, scallion, subtle spice
Mouthfeel: Clean broth, tender chicken, springy noodles

🧠 General Description:
A refined fusion ramen using traditional Bajan green seasoning as the primary flavor base, paired with a clean Japanese-style broth for balance and structure.

💵 Suggested Price:
$20–$26

📋 Menu Description:
Bajan seasoned chicken ramen, clear broth, soft egg, scallion.

🌍 Origins
Combines Barbadian green seasoning with Japanese ramen technique.

📜 History
Bajan cuisine relies heavily on green seasoning—a blend of herbs, aromatics, and peppers. Japanese ramen emphasizes broth clarity and balance.

Cultural Significance
This dish preserves Barbadian identity through seasoning while using Japanese technique to elevate structure and presentation.

🔪 Techniques
• Green seasoning marination
• Searing
• Broth clarification
• Soft boiling
• Noodle preparation

🛠️ Equipment
• Stockpot
• Sauté pan
• Mixing bowls
• Strainer
• Tongs
• Ladle

🧯 HACCP Table

HACCP Code #DescriptionH1Raw poultry storageH2Cross-contamination controlH3Temperature control

CCP Table

CCP Code #MetricIngredientPreparationCCP174°CChickenFully cookedCCP2≤5°CEggsSafe storageCCP3100°CBrothBoiled

🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime2 lb900 gChicken thighsBajan green seasoned4–12 hr4 cups950 mlChicken stock——2 tbsp30 mlSoy sauce——2 tbsp30 mlBajan green seasoningFresh blend—1 tbsp15 mlGarlicMinced—1 tbsp15 mlGingerSliced—4 portions—Ramen noodles——44EggsSoft boiled6 min22ScallionsSliced—

📖 Instructions

  1. Prepare mise en place: slice scallions, mince garlic, slice ginger, portion noodles.

  2. Coat chicken with Bajan green seasoning and marinate 4–12 hours.

  3. Sear chicken until internal temperature reaches 74°C (CCP1). Rest 10 minutes, slice.

  4. Bring stock to boil with garlic, ginger, and a small amount of green seasoning (CCP3). Reduce to simmer.

  5. Season broth lightly with soy sauce—do not overpower herbal profile.

  6. Cook noodles separately, drain well.

  7. Soft boil eggs for 6 minutes, chill immediately (CCP2), peel.

  8. Assemble: noodles → broth → sliced chicken → egg → scallions.

  9. Serve immediately.

🍽️ Plating:
Clean, minimal ramen bowl—focus on clarity and green herb tones.

📝 Notes
Green seasoning is the identity—keep it fresh, not cooked out or muted.

🧊 Storage:
Store components separately up to 3 days refrigerated.

General Description

Menu Description

Bajan seasoned chicken ramen, clear broth, soft egg, scallion.

Origins

Combines Barbadian green seasoning with Japanese ramen technique.

History

Bajan cuisine relies heavily on green seasoning—a blend of herbs, aromatics, and peppers. Japanese ramen emphasizes broth clarity and balance.

Cultural Significance

This dish preserves Barbadian identity through seasoning while using Japanese technique to elevate structure and presentation.

Techniques

Green seasoning marination

Broth clarification

Soft boiling

Noodle preparation

Equipment

Mixing bowls

HACCP

H1: Raw poultry storage

H2: Cross-contamination control

H3: Temperature control

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Chicken cooked to 74°C

CCP2: Eggs stored at or below 5°C

CCP3: Broth brought to 100°C

Ingredients

2 pounds / 900 grams chicken thighs, seasoned with Bajan green seasoning for 4–12 hours

4 cups / 950 milliliters chicken stock

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters soy sauce

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters Bajan green seasoning, fresh blend

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters garlic, minced

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters ginger, sliced

4 portions ramen noodles

4 eggs, soft-boiled for 6 minutes

2 scallions, sliced

Instructions

  1. Prepare the mise en place: slice the scallions, mince the garlic, slice the ginger, and portion the noodles.

  2. Coat the chicken with Bajan green seasoning and marinate for 4–12 hours.

  3. Sear the chicken until its internal temperature reaches 74°C. Rest for 10 minutes, then slice.

  4. Bring the chicken stock to a boil with the garlic, ginger, and a small amount of green seasoning. Reduce to a simmer.

  5. Season the broth lightly with soy sauce without overpowering the herbal profile.

  6. Cook the noodles separately and drain well.

  7. Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes, chill immediately, and peel.

  8. Assemble each bowl:

    Noodles

    Broth

    Sliced chicken

    Egg

    Scallions

  9. Serve immediately.

Plating

Clean, minimal ramen bowl with emphasis on broth clarity and green herb tones.

Notes

Green seasoning is the identity—keep it fresh, not cooked out or muted.

Storage

Store the components separately under refrigeration for up to 3 days.

snapshot.body:
Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Jerk Chicken Ramen

Cuisine: Caribbean–Japanese Fusion

Course: Main

Category: Signature Dish

Dietary Considerations: Contains gluten, soy, and egg

Yield: 4 servings

Serving Size: 1 bowl, 16 ounces or 475 milliliters

Prep Time: 30 minutes

Cook Time: 1 hour

Chill Time: 0 minutes

Rest Time: 10 minutes

Total Time: 1 hour 40 minutes

Flavor Profile

Taste: Smoky, savory, umami with balanced heat

Aroma: Jerk spice, garlic, ginger

Mouthfeel: Clean broth, tender chicken, firm noodles

General Description

A structured ramen dish where jerk-marinated chicken provides bold Caribbean flavor, supported by a clean, balanced Japanese-style broth.

Suggested Price

$20–$26

Menu Description

Jerk chicken ramen with clear broth, soft egg, and scallions.

Origins

Fusion of Jamaican jerk cooking and Japanese ramen technique.

History

Jerk seasoning originates from Jamaica’s preservation methods. Ramen is a Japanese adaptation of Chinese noodle soups focused on broth clarity.

Cultural Significance

A disciplined fusion where Caribbean identity leads and Japanese technique refines execution.

Techniques

Marination

Searing

Broth simmering

Soft boiling

Noodle cooking

Equipment

Stockpot

Sauté pan

Mixing bowls

Strainer

Tongs

Ladle

HACCP

H1: Raw poultry storage

H2: Cross-contamination control

H3: Temperature control

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Chicken cooked to 74°C

CCP2: Eggs stored and handled at or below 5°C

CCP3: Broth brought to 100°C

Ingredients

2 pounds / 900 grams chicken thighs, jerk-marinated for 4–12 hours

4 cups / 950 milliliters chicken stock

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters soy sauce

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters garlic, minced

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters ginger, sliced

4 portions ramen noodles

4 eggs, soft-boiled for 6 minutes

2 scallions, sliced

Instructions

  1. Prepare all ingredients: slice the scallions, mince the garlic, and slice the ginger.

  2. Marinate the chicken with jerk seasoning for 4–12 hours.

  3. Sear the chicken until its internal temperature reaches 74°C. Rest for 10 minutes, then slice.

  4. Bring the chicken stock to a boil with the garlic and ginger, then reduce to a simmer. Add the soy sauce.

  5. Cook the noodles separately, then drain.

  6. Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes, cool immediately, and peel.

  7. Assemble each bowl:

    Noodles

    Broth

    Sliced chicken

    Egg

    Scallions

  8. Serve immediately.

Plating

Clean bowl with centered noodles, neatly layered sliced chicken, a halved egg, and minimal garnish.

Notes

Do not overpower the broth. The jerk should be present but controlled.

Storage

Store components separately under refrigeration for up to 3 days.

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters soy sauce

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters ginger, sliced

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters garlic, crushed

4 portions ramen noodles

4 eggs, soft-boiled for 6 minutes

2 scallions, used for oil and garnish

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters neutral oil, for scallion oil

  8. Cook the noodles separately and drain well.

  9. Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes, chill immediately, and peel.

  10. Assemble each bowl:

Center the noodles.

Pour in the hot broth.

Place the sliced chicken neatly.

Add a halved soft egg.

Finish with scallion oil.

  1. Serve immediately.

snapshot.title: Jerk Chicken Ramen with Coconut-Miso Broth
snapshot.mainIdea: A Caribbean–Japanese fusion ramen combining jerk-marinated chicken with a coconut-miso broth, ramen noodles, soft egg, scallions, and chili oil.
snapshot.body:
Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Jerk Chicken Ramen with Coconut-Miso Broth

Cuisine: Caribbean–Japanese Fusion

Course: Main

Category: Signature Entrée

Dietary Considerations: Contains gluten, soy, and egg

Yield: 4 servings

Serving Size: 1 bowl, 16 ounces or 475 milliliters

Prep Time: 40 minutes

Cook Time: 1 hour 10 minutes

Chill Time: 0 minutes

Rest Time: 10 minutes

Total Time: 2 hours

Flavor Profile

Taste: Deep umami, smoky spice, mild sweetness

Aroma: Jerk spices, coconut, toasted sesame

Mouthfeel: Silky broth, tender chicken, springy noodles

General Description

A focused fusion dish that respects ramen structure while showcasing jerk-marinated chicken, supported by a balanced coconut-miso broth.

Suggested Price

$19–$25

Menu Description

Jerk chicken ramen with coconut-miso broth, soft egg, scallion, and chili oil.

Origins

Combines Jamaican jerk tradition with Japanese ramen structure.

History

Jerk cooking developed as a preservation and flavoring method in Jamaica. Ramen evolved in Japan as a structured noodle soup centered on broth technique.

Cultural Significance

This dish represents respectful fusion—Caribbean flavor remains dominant while Japanese technique provides structure and refinement.

Techniques

Marination

Grilling

Broth building

Soft boiling

Noodle blanching

Equipment

Grill or pan

Stockpot

Mixing bowls

Strainer

Tongs

Ladle

HACCP

H1: Safe poultry storage

H2: Cross-contamination prevention

H3: Proper cooking temperature

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Chicken cooked to 74°C

CCP2: Eggs stored at or below 5°C

CCP3: Broth brought to 100°C

Ingredients

2 pounds / 900 grams chicken thighs, jerk-marinated for 12–24 hours

4 cups / 950 milliliters chicken stock

1 cup / 240 milliliters coconut milk

3 tablespoons / 45 grams white miso

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters soy sauce

4 portions ramen noodles

4 eggs, soft-boiled for 6 minutes

2 scallions, sliced

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters chili oil

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters garlic, minced

1 teaspoon / 5 grams ginger, grated

Instructions

  1. Prepare all ingredients: slice the scallions, mince the garlic, and grate the ginger.

  2. Marinate the chicken in jerk seasoning for at least 12 hours.

  3. Grill or sear the chicken until its internal temperature reaches 74°C.

  4. Rest the chicken for 10 minutes, then slice.

  5. Heat the chicken stock in a pot.

  6. Add the garlic, ginger, coconut milk, and soy sauce.

  7. Bring the broth to a boil, then reduce the heat.

  8. Whisk in the miso gently. Do not boil the broth after adding the miso.

  9. Cook the noodles separately and drain.

  10. Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes, chill them in an ice bath, and peel.

  11. Assemble each bowl:

Noodles

Coconut-miso broth

Sliced jerk chicken

Halved soft egg

Scallions

Chili oil

  1. Serve immediately.

Plating

Center the noodles, fan the chicken neatly, add the halved egg, pour in the broth cleanly, and finish with scallions and chili oil.

Notes

Keep the broth balanced. Jerk is bold, so avoid overpowering the dish with miso.

Build two or three signature dishes so the menu feels cohesive rather than dependent on one dish.

Storage

Store the components separately under refrigeration for up to 3 days.

Recipe Name: Jerk Chicken Ramen with Coconut-Miso Broth
Cuisine: Jamaican-Japanese Fusion
Course: Main Course
Category: Noodle Soup

Yield: 4 servings
Serving Size: 1 bowl
Prep Time: 30 minutes
Cook Time: 45 minutes
Chill Time: 30 minutes
Rest Time: 5 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 50 minutes
Flavor Profile:
Taste: Spicy, savory, mildly sweet, tangy, and deeply umami
Aroma: Allspice, thyme, scallion, ginger, garlic, toasted sesame, and coconut
Mouthfeel: Silky broth, tender chicken, springy noodles, and crisp vegetables

🧠 General Description:

This fusion ramen combines Jamaican jerk-seasoned chicken with a creamy coconut-miso broth. Aromatic spices, Scotch bonnet chile, ginger, garlic, and thyme create a bold foundation, while miso and soy sauce contribute balanced umami. Springy ramen noodles, fresh vegetables, a soft-cooked egg, and sliced jerk chicken complete the bowl.

💵 Suggested Price:

$19–$24 per serving

📋 Menu Description:

Jerk-spiced chicken, ramen noodles, vegetables, and soft egg in a silky coconut-miso broth with scallions, lime, and sesame.

🌍 Origins

This dish is a contemporary fusion of Jamaican jerk cooking and Japanese ramen. Jamaican jerk traditionally features allspice, thyme, chile, scallion, and aromatic spices, while ramen centers on wheat noodles served in a seasoned broth with composed toppings.

📜 History

Jerk cooking developed in Jamaica through Indigenous Taíno preservation techniques and the culinary practices of Maroon communities. Traditional jerk was cooked slowly over aromatic wood, producing highly seasoned meat with a distinctive smoky character. Japanese ramen evolved from Chinese-style wheat noodle soups and developed into numerous regional forms distinguished by their broths, seasonings, noodles, and toppings.

Cultural Significance

Jerk is an important expression of Jamaican culinary identity, recognized for its assertive seasoning, chile heat, and communal cooking traditions. Ramen holds a similarly prominent place in Japanese food culture, where careful broth preparation and regional variation are central to the dish. This recipe respectfully combines characteristic elements of both traditions without presenting itself as a traditional version of either cuisine.

  • Marinating

  • Searing

  • Oven roasting

  • Aromatic sweating

  • Broth infusion

  • Tempering miso

  • Soft-boiling eggs

  • Blanching vegetables

  • Noodle cooking

  • Bias slicing

  • Chef’s knife

  • Cutting board

  • Mixing bowls

  • Whisk

  • Fine-mesh strainer

  • Large saucepan or stockpot

  • Medium saucepan

  • Oven-safe skillet or sheet pan

  • Instant-read probe thermometer

  • Tongs

  • Ladle

  • Colander

snapshot.title: Plantain Gyoza
snapshot.mainIdea: A Japanese-Caribbean fusion dumpling combining Japanese gyoza technique with a sweet-savory filling of ripe plantain, cabbage, scallions, ginger, garlic, soy sauce, sesame oil, and mild chile.
snapshot.body:
Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Plantain Gyoza

Cuisine: Japanese-Caribbean Fusion

Course: Appetizer

Category: Dumplings

Dietary Considerations: Vegetarian

Yield: 24 gyoza

Serving Size: 4 gyoza

Prep Time: 30 minutes

Cook Time: 20 minutes

Chill Time: 15 minutes

Rest Time: 10 minutes

Total Time: 1 hour 15 minutes

Flavor Profile

Taste: Sweet-savory plantain, ginger, scallion, soy, and mild chile

Aroma: Toasted sesame, caramelized plantain, garlic, and fresh scallion

Mouthfeel: Crisp-bottomed wrappers with tender, creamy filling

General Description

Plantain gyoza combine Japanese dumpling technique with a savory filling of ripe plantain, cabbage, aromatics, soy sauce, and sesame oil. The dumplings are pan-seared, steamed, and finished uncovered for crisp bottoms and tender tops.

Suggested Price

$9.00–$12.00 per 6-piece appetizer

Menu Description

Crisp-bottomed gyoza filled with sweet plantain, cabbage, ginger, scallion, sesame, and chile, served with a tangy soy dipping sauce.

Origins

Gyoza developed in Japan from Chinese jiaozi and became known for thin wrappers, finely textured fillings, and the pan-sear-and-steam cooking method.

This version incorporates plantain, a staple ingredient throughout the Caribbean, Latin America, West Africa, and parts of Southeast Asia.

History

Japanese gyoza became widely popular during the twentieth century, particularly after Japanese cooks adapted Chinese dumplings into smaller, thinner-skinned parcels with pronounced garlic and crisp seared bottoms.

Plantains have been cultivated and cooked for centuries across tropical regions and are used in both savory and sweet preparations.

Cultural Significance

Plantain gyoza represent a fusion of Japanese dumpling craftsmanship and tropical plantain cookery. The dish demonstrates how familiar techniques can carry ingredients from different culinary traditions while preserving the defining texture and service style of gyoza.

Techniques

Fine vegetable chopping

Plantain mashing

Moisture reduction

Dumpling filling and pleating

Pan-searing

Covered steaming

Sauce emulsification

Equipment

Chef’s knife

Cutting board

Mixing bowls

Fork or potato masher

Measuring cups and spoons

Digital kitchen scale

Small skillet

Large nonstick skillet with lid

Heat-resistant spatula

Small whisk

Sheet tray

Parchment paper

HACCP

HACCP-1: Wash produce under clean running water and prevent cross-contamination from contaminated utensils, hands, or work surfaces.

HACCP-2: Cool the cooked filling promptly before assembling the gyoza to limit bacterial growth and prevent wrapper deterioration.

HACCP-3: Cook the assembled gyoza thoroughly until the filling reaches at least 165°F / 74°C.

HACCP-4: Hold the prepared filling and assembled uncooked gyoza at or below 41°F / 5°C until cooking.

HACCP-5: Refrigerate cooked leftovers within 2 hours and reheat them to 165°F / 74°C before service.

HACCP-6: Prevent allergen cross-contact involving wheat, soy, and sesame during preparation and service.

Critical Control Points

CCP-1: Cold Holding

Critical Control Point: Cold holding of prepared filling and assembled gyoza

Hazard: Biological growth from time-temperature abuse

Critical Limit: Maintain at or below 41°F / 5°C

Monitoring: Check the product temperature with a calibrated thermometer before assembly and cooking.

Corrective Action: Rapidly chill product that has remained above 41°F / 5°C for no more than 2 hours. Discard when the time or temperature is uncertain.

Verification: Supervisor reviews temperature readings and refrigeration practices.

Records: Cold-holding temperature log

CCP-2: Final Cooking

Critical Control Point: Final cooking of gyoza

Hazard: Survival of biological pathogens

Critical Limit: Filling must reach at least 165°F / 74°C

Monitoring: Insert a sanitized probe thermometer into representative gyoza from each batch.

Corrective Action: Continue cooking until 165°F / 74°C is reached. Discard any batch that cannot be safely corrected.

Verification: Verify thermometer calibration and review cooking temperatures.

Records: Cooking-temperature log

CCP-3: Cooling and Storage

Critical Control Point: Cooling and storage of cooked leftovers

Hazard: Biological growth during improper cooling

Critical Limit: Cool from 135°F to 70°F / 57°C to 21°C within 2 hours and from 70°F to 41°F / 21°C to 5°C within 4 additional hours.

Monitoring: Check and document temperatures during cooling.

Corrective Action: Divide the gyoza into shallow containers, increase airflow, or use an ice bath. Discard if cooling limits are exceeded.

Verification: Supervisor reviews cooling records and storage conditions.

Records: Cooling log and date label

Ingredients

1 large / 300 grams ripe plantain, peeled and cut into ½-inch pieces — 5 minutes preparation

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters neutral cooking oil, divided — 1 minute preparation

1 cup / 90 grams green cabbage, finely chopped — 5 minutes preparation

3 / 30 grams scallions, thinly sliced — 2 minutes preparation

2 teaspoons / 10 grams fresh ginger, finely grated — 2 minutes preparation

2 cloves / 6 grams garlic, minced — 2 minutes preparation

1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters soy sauce, measured — 1 minute preparation

1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters toasted sesame oil, measured — 1 minute preparation

1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters rice vinegar, measured — 1 minute preparation

½ teaspoon / 2 grams crushed red pepper flakes, measured — 1 minute preparation

¼ teaspoon / 1 gram fine sea salt, measured — 1 minute preparation

24 / 240 grams round gyoza wrappers, kept covered to prevent drying — 1 minute preparation

½ cup / 120 milliliters water, for steaming — 1 minute preparation

¼ cup / 60 milliliters soy sauce, for dipping sauce — 1 minute preparation

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters rice vinegar, for dipping sauce — 1 minute preparation

1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters toasted sesame oil, for dipping sauce — 1 minute preparation

1 teaspoon / 5 grams brown sugar, for dipping sauce — 1 minute preparation

1 teaspoon / 5 grams scallion greens, thinly sliced for garnish — 1 minute preparation

1 teaspoon / 3 grams toasted sesame seeds, for garnish — 1 minute preparation

Instructions

  1. Wash the cabbage, scallions, ginger, and plantain under clean running water as appropriate. Sanitize the work surface and organize all ingredients and equipment.

  2. Heat 2 teaspoons / 10 milliliters of the neutral oil in a small skillet over medium heat.

  3. Add the diced plantain and cook for 5–7 minutes, stirring frequently, until tender and lightly caramelized.

  4. Transfer the plantain to a mixing bowl and mash it with a fork, leaving a few small pieces for texture.

  5. Add the remaining 1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters neutral oil to the skillet.

  6. Add the cabbage, scallions, ginger, garlic, and crushed red pepper flakes.

  7. Cook the vegetables for 3–4 minutes, stirring frequently, until softened and the excess moisture has evaporated.

  8. Add the cooked vegetable mixture to the mashed plantain.

  9. Stir in 1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters soy sauce, 1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters toasted sesame oil, 1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters rice vinegar, and the fine sea salt.

  10. Spread the filling in a shallow container and refrigerate for 15 minutes until cooled to or below 41°F / 5°C before prolonged holding.

  11. Place one gyoza wrapper on a clean work surface. Keep the remaining wrappers covered with a slightly damp towel.

  12. Spoon approximately 2 teaspoons / 10 grams of filling into the center of the wrapper.

  13. Moisten the wrapper edge lightly with water, fold it in half, and pleat one side while pressing firmly against the opposite edge to seal.

  14. Place the completed gyoza on a parchment-lined tray and cover it while filling and pleating the remaining wrappers.

  15. Refrigerate the assembled gyoza at or below 41°F / 5°C until ready to cook.

  16. Whisk together ¼ cup / 60 milliliters soy sauce, 2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters rice vinegar, 1 teaspoon / 5 milliliters toasted sesame oil, and the brown sugar until the sugar dissolves.

  17. Heat a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat and lightly coat the surface with neutral oil when needed.

  18. Arrange the gyoza flat-side down in a single layer without crowding.

  19. Sear for 2–3 minutes until the bottoms are golden brown.

  20. Carefully add ½ cup / 120 milliliters water and immediately cover the skillet.

  21. Steam the gyoza for 5–6 minutes.

  22. Remove the lid and continue cooking for 2–3 minutes until the water evaporates and the bottoms become crisp.

  23. Check representative gyoza with a sanitized thermometer and confirm that the center of the filling reaches at least 165°F / 74°C.

  24. Continue cooking any gyoza that have not reached 165°F / 74°C.

  25. Arrange the fully cooked gyoza on a serving plate with the crisp sides facing upward.

  26. Garnish with sliced scallion greens and toasted sesame seeds.

  27. Serve immediately with the prepared dipping sauce.

Plating

Arrange 4–6 gyoza in a slightly overlapping row or circular fan with the crisp golden surfaces visible.

Serve the dipping sauce in a small bowl.

Finish with scallion greens and toasted sesame seeds.

Notes

Use a ripe plantain with mostly black skin for a sweeter, creamier filling.

Use a yellow plantain with black spots for a firmer, more savory result.

Cook the cabbage until excess moisture evaporates to prevent soggy wrappers.

Do not overfill the gyoza because the seams may open during steaming.

Keep unused wrappers covered because they dry quickly when exposed to air.

Storage

Store uncooked assembled gyoza in a covered container at or below 41°F / 5°C for up to 24 hours.

Freeze uncooked gyoza in a single layer until solid, then transfer them to a sealed freezer container for up to 1 month.

Cook frozen gyoza without thawing, adding 2–3 minutes to the steaming time.

Refrigerate cooked leftovers within 2 hours and consume within 3 days.

Cool cooked leftovers from 135°F to 70°F / 57°C to 21°C within 2 hours and from 70°F to 41°F / 21°C to 5°C within 4 additional hours.

Reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C before serving.

revisions.content:
Japanese techniques can refine Caribbean flavors without losing identity:

  • Tempura → light fry for things like plantain, saltfish fritters

  • Tataki → lightly seared jerk tuna or snapper

  • Ramen structure → Caribbean broths (oxtail, goat) turned into ramen

  • Pickling (tsukemono) → quick-pickled mango, papaya, or Scotch bonnet

  • Yakitori style grilling → jerk skewers with tare glaze

revisions.title: Golden Coconut Curry–Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Creamer Potatoes
revisions.content:
• Brooklyn Delhi Indian Simmer Sauce, Golden Coconut Curry $5.00 1/4 cup 12oz @.50c Fresh Direct

  • Shredded Brussels Sprouts 10 oz $5.49 Fresh Direct

  • The Little Potato Company Fresh Creamer Potatoes, Little Yellows 1.5 bag $4.49 Fresh Direct

  • Olive oil 2 tbsp

  • dehydrated onion 1/4 cup

  • dehydrated sweet pepper 1/3 cup

  • Salt TT

  • Papper TT

Recipe Name: Golden Coconut Curry–Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Creamer Potatoes
Cuisine: Indian-Inspired American
Course: Main Course or Side Dish
Category: Roasted Vegetables
Dietary Considerations: Vegan, Vegetarian, Dairy-Free
Yield: 6 servings
Serving Size: Approximately 10 oz (284 g)
Prep Time: 15 minutes
Cook Time: 30 minutes
Chill Time: N/A
Rest Time: 5 minutes
Total Time: 50 minutes
Flavor Profile:
Taste: Savory, mildly sweet, warmly spiced, and lightly salty
Aroma: Toasted coconut, turmeric, roasted onion, and caramelized vegetables
Mouthfeel: Crisp-edged Brussels sprouts, creamy potatoes, and a rich curry coating

🧠 General Description:

A high-temperature convection-roasted vegetable dish featuring tender yellow creamer potatoes, caramelized shredded Brussels sprouts, dehydrated onion, sweet pepper, and Brooklyn Delhi Golden Coconut Curry sauce. The sauce adds coconut richness, ginger, turmeric, lemon, and gentle warming spices.

💵 Suggested Price:

$9.00 per serving as a vegetable entrée or $6.00 per serving as a shared side dish.

📋 Menu Description:

Crispy Brussels sprouts and creamy yellow potatoes roasted with golden coconut curry, sweet peppers, onion, and aromatic spices.

🌍 Origins

This dish combines Indian-inspired coconut curry flavors with the Western technique of high-temperature sheet-pan roasting. Coconut-based curries are common throughout southern India and neighboring regions, while roasted Brussels sprouts and creamer potatoes reflect contemporary American vegetable cookery.

📜 History

Coconut, turmeric, ginger, onion, and aromatic spices have long been used in regional South Asian cooking. Prepared simmer sauces translate these established flavor combinations into convenient modern formats. Roasting the sauce with vegetables concentrates its flavors and creates caramelized edges that differ from the softer consistency of a traditionally simmered curry.

Cultural Significance

The recipe represents a contemporary fusion approach in which traditional South Asian flavor profiles are applied to readily available vegetables and modern convection-oven techniques. It also demonstrates how a prepared curry sauce can serve as both a seasoning and a roasting glaze.

🔪 Techniques

  • High-temperature convection roasting

  • Par-cooking potatoes for even doneness

  • Rehydrating dried vegetables

  • Tossing and coating

  • Sheet-pan spacing

  • Mid-roast turning

  • Resting before service

🛠️ Equipment

  • Convection oven

  • Large rimmed sheet pan

  • Parchment paper or silicone baking mat

  • Large mixing bowl

  • Small heat-resistant bowl

  • Colander

  • Measuring cups

  • Measuring spoons

  • Chef’s knife

  • Cutting board

  • Flexible spatula

  • Instant-read thermometer

🧯 HACCP Table

HACCP Code #DescriptionHACCP-1Wash hands, sanitize equipment, and inspect the Brussels sprouts and potatoes before preparation.HACCP-2Prevent cross-contamination by using clean utensils, bowls, and cutting surfaces.HACCP-3Roast the vegetables until the potatoes are tender and the dish reaches at least 165°F (74°C) before service.HACCP-4Hold the finished dish at 135°F (57°C) or above when it is not served immediately.HACCP-5Cool leftovers from 135°F to 70°F (57°C to 21°C) within 2 hours and from 70°F to 41°F (21°C to 5°C) within an additional 4 hours.HACCP-6Refrigerate opened curry sauce and cooked leftovers at 41°F (5°C) or below.

CCP Table

CCP Code #Critical Control PointHazardCritical LimitMonitoringCorrective ActionVerificationRecordsN/ANo true CCP identified for immediate preparation and serviceN/AN/AFollow established sanitation, cooking, holding, cooling, and storage proceduresCorrect any observed time, temperature, sanitation, or storage deviationReview preparation and storage practicesProduction and cooling logs when applicable

🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime1 bag, 1.5 lb680 gLittle Potato Company Little Yellows Fresh Creamer PotatoesWashed, drained, and halved if large5 minutes1 package, 10 oz284 gShredded Brussels sproutsInspected and separated2 minutes1/4 cup60 mLBrooklyn Delhi Golden Coconut Curry Simmer SauceStirred before measuring1 minute2 tablespoons30 mLOlive oilDivided1 minute1/4 cup20 gDehydrated onionRehydrated and drained10 minutes1/3 cup25 gDehydrated sweet pepperRehydrated and drained10 minutesTo tasteTo tasteSaltAdded gradually1 minuteTo tasteTo tasteBlack pepperFreshly ground if available1 minute

📖 Instructions

  1. Preheat a convection oven to 450°F (232°C). Position a rack in the center of the oven and line a large rimmed sheet pan with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

  2. Place the dehydrated onion and dehydrated sweet pepper in a heat-resistant bowl. Cover them with hot water and allow them to rehydrate for 10 minutes. Drain thoroughly and press out excess water.

  3. Wash and inspect the creamer potatoes. Halve any potatoes that are larger than approximately 1 inch (2.5 cm) in diameter so the pieces cook evenly.

  4. Place the potatoes in a microwave-safe covered container with 2 tablespoons (30 mL) water. Microwave for 5 to 7 minutes, or until slightly tender but not fully cooked. Drain well. Alternatively, simmer them in water for 8 to 10 minutes and drain thoroughly.

  5. Combine the par-cooked potatoes, shredded Brussels sprouts, rehydrated onion, rehydrated sweet pepper, olive oil, salt, and black pepper in a large mixing bowl.

  6. Add the Golden Coconut Curry Simmer Sauce and toss until the vegetables are evenly coated.

  7. Spread the mixture across the prepared sheet pan in a shallow, even layer. Turn the potatoes cut-side down and avoid overcrowding the Brussels sprouts.

  8. Roast at 450°F (232°C) on convection for 15 minutes.

  9. Remove the pan from the oven and turn the potatoes and Brussels sprouts with a flexible spatula. Redistribute any vegetables that are browning more quickly around the edges.

  10. Return the pan to the oven and roast for an additional 12 to 15 minutes, until the potatoes are tender, the Brussels sprouts have crisp caramelized edges, and the sauce is concentrated around the vegetables.

  11. Confirm that the center of the dish has reached at least 165°F (74°C). Remove the sheet pan from the oven.

  12. Taste and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper as needed.

  13. Allow the vegetables to rest on the sheet pan for 5 minutes so the curry coating thickens slightly and adheres to the vegetables.

  14. Transfer to a warmed serving platter or portion directly onto individual plates. Serve immediately.

🍽️ Plating:

Arrange the potatoes through the center of a shallow warmed bowl and mound the roasted Brussels sprouts over and around them. Spoon any concentrated curry mixture from the sheet pan over the vegetables. Finish with freshly ground black pepper. For added color, garnish with fresh cilantro or thinly sliced scallions when available.

📝 Notes

  • Par-cooking the potatoes helps them become creamy inside during the same roasting time required to caramelize the shredded Brussels sprouts.

  • Drain the rehydrated onion and peppers thoroughly. Excess water can steam the vegetables and reduce browning.

  • Use a sufficiently large sheet pan. Overcrowding traps moisture and produces softer vegetables.

  • The curry sauce contains coconut cream, ginger, turmeric, lemon, onion, garlic, and spices, giving the dish richness and mild aromatic heat.

  • The nutritional estimate assumes six servings and approximately 1 teaspoon of added salt for the complete recipe.

  • The stated ingredient cost is approximately $15.98 before accounting for salt, pepper, and any delivery charges.

🧊 Storage:

Cool leftovers promptly in shallow containers. Refrigerate at 41°F (5°C) or below for up to 4 days. Reheat uncovered in a 400°F (204°C) convection oven for 8 to 12 minutes, or until the center reaches 165°F (74°C). The dish may be frozen for up to 2 months, although the Brussels sprouts and potatoes may soften after thawing.

snapshot.title: Letter to My Younger Self
snapshot.mainIdea: I have to write a letter to my younger self apologizing for calling him weak, virtue-less, immoral, and not who he claimed to be because he broke his moral code. I need to confront how harshly I judged him and recognize the pain, circumstances, vulnerability, and humanity behind his actions.
snapshot.body:
The letter should acknowledge that I judged my younger self by the worst moment of his life. I called him weak, virtueless, immoral, and false because he acted against the moral code he believed defined him.

The apology should not deny what happened or remove accountability. It should recognize the difference between breaking a moral code and having no morals. One failure does not erase a person’s character, values, or previous efforts to live according to those values.

I need to examine why I believed shame and condemnation were necessary. I may have called him weak because I could not accept his vulnerability or the circumstances in which cocaine was introduced to him. I judged him without fully understanding what he was carrying, what condition he was in, or what led him to that moment.

The letter should speak to him with the understanding and compassion I did not give him then. It should acknowledge that he was still responsible for his choices while also recognizing that responsibility does not require lifelong self-hatred.

The central principle is that violating a moral code does not automatically make someone immoral, virtueless, or fraudulent. Accountability should identify the wrong without reducing the entire person to that wrong.

The letter should end with forgiveness, accountability, and permission for him—and for me—to become more than that moment.

I need to confront how harshly I judged him and recognize the pain, circumstances, and humanity behind his actions

questions: Why did I believe one failure erased everything good in him?
What did I mean when I called him weak?
Was I condemning him because I could not accept my own vulnerability?
What circumstances surrounded the decision he made?
How can I acknowledge wrongdoing without defining him entirely by it?
What would accountability look like without shame or self-hatred?
What does he need to hear from me now?
What part of him am I actually trying to forgive?
Can a person break a moral code and still remain a moral person?
What permission do I need to give him—and myself—to move forward?

revisions.title: The Path in the Therapist’s Office
revisions.content: "A calendar image in my therapist’s office caught my attention. It shows a wooden path running through sand and tall grass toward a quiet beach, framed by palm trees and sunlight. I need to write a story or poem based on how the image came to me in that moment—not simply describe the scene, but explore why I noticed it, what I felt while looking at it, and what the path seemed to be opening toward.

I need to write a story or poem based on how the image came to me in that moment—not simply describe the scene, but explore why I noticed it, what I felt while looking at it, and what the path seemed to be opening toward.
notes: Begin with the image hanging in the therapist’s office rather than beginning on the beach.
Explore why this particular image held my attention at that moment.
The wooden path may suggest movement, transition, escape, return, healing, or uncertainty, but do not decide its meaning before writing.
Consider the contrast between sitting in the office and looking out at an open landscape.
The sunlight enters strongly from the left while the path continues toward a calmer horizon.
Ask whether the path feels like an invitation, a memory, a destination, or something I am not yet ready to enter.
The story or poem should come from my emotional response to the image, not from a generic description of a tropical beach.
Possible opening thought: I noticed the path before I noticed the sea.
